title: Eviction and LRU
summary: What a full cache throws away to make room, why least recently used is the usual answer, and where it goes wrong.

blocks.p: A cache is smaller than the data behind it. Once it is full, every miss that adds a new item must remove an old one. Removing an item to make room is called **eviction**.
The choice matters. Evict an item that is about to be read again and the next read misses. Evict an item nobody needs and the cache keeps working.

The ideal policy evicts the item that will next be used furthest in the future. László Bélády described it in [a 1966 study of replacement algorithms](https://doi.org/10.1147/sj.52.0078). It can't be built, because it needs to know future requests. Real policies guess from the past.

**LRU** evicts the item that was read longest ago. The guess is that something read recently will be read again soon. Each read moves the item to the front. A new item goes in at the front, and the item at the back is evicted.

blocks.caption: A cache with 4 slots, kept in order of last use. Each hit moves a letter to the front. Each miss adds one at the front and evicts the one at the back.

list: **FIFO**, first in first out, evicts the oldest item, however often it was read. It is simpler, but it throws out popular items on schedule.
**Random** evicts any item. It needs no bookkeeping at all and does better than you might expect.
**LFU**, least frequently used, evicts the item with the fewest reads. It keeps steady favourites, but it can hold on to items that were popular long ago.

blocks.caption: A is read every second request. LRU never evicts it. FIFO evicts it when it becomes the oldest entry.

blocks.p: One large scan, such as a report that reads every item once, fills an LRU cache with items nobody will read again. The scan evicts the popular items, and they all miss afterwards.

blocks.caption: A and B are popular. A one-off scan of C, D, E and F pushes them out, so they miss when they are read again.

list: **Redis lets you choose.** Its [eviction settings](https://redis.io/docs/latest/develop/reference/eviction/) include LRU, LFU, random, and evicting the keys closest to expiry, either across all keys or only keys with a TTL.

**Redis approximates LRU.** Keeping every key in exact order costs memory, so Redis samples a few keys and evicts the least recently used among them. The same page describes how close the approximation gets.
**Exact LRU is cheap for small caches.** A hash map plus a linked list gives constant time lookups and moves. Many in-process caches use this.
**Measure, then choose.** Which policy wins depends on the access pattern. Measure the hit ratio on real traffic before changing the default.

blocks.p: 50 keys, a few of them popular. Change the cache size and the eviction policy, and compare hit ratios.

blocks.caption: With 10 slots, try LRU, FIFO and random. Then give the cache 40 slots and see the policies converge.

list: A full cache must evict an item for every new one.
The ideal choice is the item needed furthest in the future, which no real cache knows.
LRU evicts the item read longest ago, and suits most workloads.
A one-off scan can flush an LRU cache. LFU and other policies resist that.

references.label: L. A. Bélády: A study of replacement algorithms for a virtual-storage computer (1966)
references.note: The optimal policy: evict what is needed furthest in the future.
